paper.title: Accelerating the Discovery of Hybrid Perovskites with Targeted Band Gaps via Interpretable Machine Learning
paper.file_name: 36_Accelerating the Discovery of Hybrid Perovskites with Targeted Band Gaps via Interpretable Machine Learning.pdf
paper.research_summary: This study combined feature engineering, the gradient-boosted regression tree (GBRT) algorithm, and the genetic algorithm-based symbolic regression (GASR) algorithm to develop an interpretable machine learning (ML) strategy for predicting the band gap of hybrid organic−inorganic perovskites (HOIPs) accurately and quantitatively interpreting the factors affecting the band gap. Seven best physical features were selected to construct a GBRT model with a root-mean-square error of less than 0.060 eV, and the most important feature is the electronegativity difference between the B-site and the X-site (χB−X). Further, a mathematical formula (Eg = χB−X^2 + 0.881χB−X) was constructed with GASR for a quantitative interpretation of the band gap influence patterns. According to the ML model, the HOIP MA0.23FA0.02Cs0.75Pb0.59Sn0.41Br0.24I2.76 was obtained, with a suitable band gap of 1.39 eV.

tasks.task_name_raw: predicting the experimental band gap values of HOIPs
tasks.objective: Predict the experimental band gap values of hybrid organic−inorganic perovskites (HOIPs) using an interpretable ML strategy
material_scope: ABX3 structure (A = Cs, FA, or MA; B = Pb or Sn; X = Br, Cl, or I)
input_requirements: physical features (e.g., electronegativity, ionic radius, Goldschmidt tolerance factor, octahedral factor, electron affinity, dipole polarizability, atomic radius, d/f orbital electrons)
output_goal: interpretable quantitative relationship (mathematical formula) between physical features and band gap

evidence.text: To address the challenges of a “black box” for perovskite band gap prediction, the focus of this work is to predict the experimental band gap values of HOIPs using an interpretable ML strategy.

stages.stage_goal: Ensure quantity and accuracy of experimental band gap data for HOIPs
stage_output: 610 data points with known band gap values

evidence.text: To ensure the quantity and accuracy of the data, two principles were used in the data collection and cleaning process. First, we selected compounds with a three-dimensional structure of ABX3 (A-site = Cs, FA, or MA; B-site = Pb or Sn; X-site = Br, Cl, or I). Second, for data with the same composition but different band gaps, we chose the average value when the difference between the maximum value and the minimum value is less than 0.2 eV. When it is greater than 0.2 eV, we chose the model because the experimental error is about 0.1−0.2 eV when using different instruments. All data points were collated from the PSC database built by Jacobsson et al.16 Eventually, the total data set consists of 610 data points with known band gap values.

stages.stage_goal: Partition dataset into training and test sets for model evaluation

evidence.text: Then, we randomly divided 15% of the data set as the test set to evaluate the generalization capability for all ML models, and the remaining 85% as the training set to train all ML models.

stages.stage_goal: Construct physically meaningful features to replace atomic ratios and reduce dimensionality
stage_input: nine element characteristics (electronegativity, tolerance factor, ionic radius, etc.)

evidence.text: In order to validate the accuracy of the data set and comparison with the subsequent model with physical features as input, we simultaneously trained models with composition (ML-C) as features... To further enhance the physical interpretability, we used physical features to replace the simple atomic ratio features as the model inputs (ML-P)... In this work, we chose nine element characteristics as descriptors in the initial feature pool based on a priori knowledge... In addition to the individual descriptors, we considered their sums, differences, and ratios to create new features, named feature crosses... When the model input contains many highly correlated features, it will increase the dimensionality of the feature space and lead to unnecessary complexity in the resulting model. In order to reduce model complexity to improve the model accuracy and to reduce the model training time, we reduced the dimensionality of the new features in two steps. First step, we subject these features to a correlation filter to classify the highly correlated features by Pearson correlation coefficient analysis... Those features with a Pearson correlation coefficient greater than 0.95 are considered as highly correlated ones and are thus classified into one group; only one of the features was retained for each group... After that, 11 groups of highly correlated features were identified, and 11 features are retained as listed in Table 1. The second step is to filter the optimal subfeatures... Figure 3b shows the variation of GBRT-P accuracy with the number of subfeatures; the model accuracy is not significantly improved when the number of subfeatures is greater than 7, so we chose the top 7 features in ranked feature importance as input variables...

stages.stage_goal: Train high-performance, interpretable band gap prediction model using physical features

evidence.text: Figure 3b shows the variation of GBRT-P accuracy with the number of subfeatures; the model accuracy is not significantly improved when the number of subfeatures is greater than 7, so we chose the top 7 features in ranked feature importance as input variables to reduce the complexity of the model without sacrificing the accuracy too much and the final GBRT-P model with an RMSE of 0.059 eV for the test set.

stages.stage_goal: Derive interpretable mathematical formula relating physical features to band gap

evidence.text: To explicitly obtain the mapping between physical features and the band gap, we used the GASR algorithm to develop mathematical formulas between 7 features and band gaps... After trading off the complexity and accuracy of the formula, we chose the formula Eg = χB−X^2 + 0.881χB−X as the best formula with the highest accuracy, RMSE = 0.84 eV for the test set, and the lowest complexity was 3.

stages.stage_goal: Generate candidate HOIP compositions with targeted band gaps using GBRT-P predictions
stage_output: compositions with band gaps in 1.3−1.4 eV and 1.7−2.1 eV ranges

evidence.text: In this work, GBRT-P was used for band gap prediction for composition screening, which has both high accuracy and interpretability. We focused on the ideal band gap range (1.3−1.4 eV) and wide band gap range (1.7−2.1 eV) to find potential compositions... We constructed the prediction set MAaFAbCs1−a−bPbxSn1−xBrmI1−m (a, b, x, m = 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03...1), In total, there are about 5.2 × 107 compounds in the search space as the prediction set... a random selection of 100,000 compositions which has the same feature space distribution as the initial prediction set was made for prediction using GBRT-P. Then, we selected compositions that are not in the original data set and whose band gaps are distributed in the range of 1.3−1.4 and 1.7−2.1 eV.

stages.stage_goal: Select three novel compositions for experimental synthesis from screened candidates

evidence.text: Finally, we randomly selected three groups among the remaining compositions for the experimental synthesis. As can be seen in Figure 4a, we selected compositions in the original data set with sparse distribution of data points and located in three different band gap ranges, which can better demonstrate the predictive power of the model.

stages.stage_name_raw: experimental synthesis and band gap measurement
stages.stage_goal: Validate predicted band gaps through experimental synthesis and UV−vis spectroscopy

evidence.text: Three compositions were experimentally synthesized, and the XRD results are presented in Figure 4b, indicating that all three compositions possess pure perovskite structures. The band gap values, measured by UV−vis spectra, are shown in Figure 4c.
